summary: Describes how chains of proxies can pass authentication and accounting requests between organizations in roaming services such as dial-up access, and how policies can be applied along the way. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When you visit another city, your key card gets checked by a series of desks that pass your question back to your home office. This describes how those desks cooperate.

questions: what is the network access identifier
subtitle: Why roaming networks pass RADIUS requests through chains of proxies, and what that costs in trust.

tldr.problem: In roaming, a user's request must reach a home server run by another organization, and a network access server cannot easily reach every partner directly.
tldr.mechanism: Requests and accounting packets travel through a chain of RADIUS proxies chosen from the Network Access Identifier, and the proxies can adjust attributes, apply policy and store accounting data.
tldr.outcome: The mechanisms were in use, but the RFC warns that they are open to attack and to fraud by roaming partners, so they are not suitable for wide-scale deployment on the Internet.

today: RFC 2607 is an Informational memo from June 1999, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself says these methods are not suitable for wide-scale deployment on the Internet.

sections.title: Proxy Chaining in Roaming
sections.content:
The RFC explains that proxy chaining was widely deployed to provide roaming services. Authentication, authorization and accounting packets are routed between a Network Access Server (NAS) and a home server through a series of proxies. The home server must be consulted for password-based authentication because it holds the password database.

A RADIUS proxy looks like a RADIUS server to the NAS and like a RADIUS client to the next server. Routing relies on structure in the user ID, called the Network Access Identifier (NAI). The set of relationships between the local ISP's proxy and the home server is the roaming relationship path. The memo states that the mechanisms described are in current use.
sections.plainLanguage: Your request is passed from desk to desk until it reaches your home office, and the answer comes back the same way.

sections.title: What Proxies Are Used For
sections.content:
The RFC lists six functions of proxies. Scalability: since RADIUS needs a shared secret for each client-server pair, a consortium of 100 partners connecting directly would need 4950 shared secrets, but with a central proxy only 100. Authentication forwarding: most NAS devices have no forwarding logic, so a proxy forwards based on the NAI. How a proxy learns the NAI-to-home-server mapping is out of scope.

Capabilities adjustment: RADIUS has no capabilities negotiation, so a proxy may add, delete or change attributes in an Access-Accept to suit the NAS, for example when a static IP address would not be routable there. This can lead to disputes if the service differs from what the home server asked for. Policy implementation: for example, limiting a partner to certain hours on a NAS. A proxy doing this acts as a man in the middle.

Accounting reliability: with four systems and a one percent failure rate on each hop, 3.9 percent of accounting transactions can be lost, and an accounting proxy near the NAS can store records and retry. Atomic operation: proxies can deliver accounting data serially so all parties receive it.
sections.plainLanguage: The middle desks help in several ways. They cut down on the number of secret keys needed, adjust the answer to fit the local gate, and enforce the rules of the visit.

sections.title: Request Flow and Policy Rules
sections.content:
A request goes from the NAS to Proxy1, to Proxy2, to the home server. The reply returns along the same chain, with each proxy matching the reply to the request it sent. Except in two cases, a proxy SHOULD NOT reply without first receiving a reply from the home server. The two cases are enforcing policy and acting as an accounting store.

A proxy enforcing policy MAY answer an Access-Request itself, but only with an Access-Reject or an Access-Challenge. It MUST NOT answer with an Access-Accept. A proxy MAY also reject a request the home server accepted. It then SHOULD send the NAS an Access-Reject and send the home server an Accounting-Request with Acct-Status-Type=Proxy-Stop (6), so the home server knows the session was denied downstream. A proxy MUST NOT send an Access-Accept after receiving an Access-Reject.
sections.plainLanguage: A middle desk can say no on its own, but it is never allowed to say yes on behalf of the home office.

sections.title: Accounting Behavior
sections.content:
A proxy SHOULD route an Accounting-Request along the same realm path used for authentication, though not necessarily through the same machines. The Class attribute ties accounting to earlier authentication: home servers SHOULD put a unique session identifier in it in an Access-Accept and Access-Challenge, proxies and NASes MUST forward it unmodified, and the NAS MUST include it in later requests, especially Accounting-Requests.

A proxy MUST forward all Accounting Requests and MUST guarantee that the end server and all intermediate servers receive them. It can do this by withholding its reply until the upstream reply arrives, which makes the transaction atomic, or by acting as a store point that re-forwards until it gets a reply. Store and forward is not atomic, so audit logs may not reconcile, which opens room for fraud. A proxy can also flood an Accounting-Request with Acct-Status-Type=Accounting-Off (8) to every realm it forwards to when a NAS is shutting down.
sections.plainLanguage: The visit ticket carries a number that every desk keeps, so the bill at the end can be matched to the visit it belongs to.

sections.title: Security Weaknesses
sections.content:
RADIUS was designed for use inside one administrative domain, where proxies are trusted. Roaming is inter-domain, so proxies cannot necessarily be trusted, and RADIUS offers no end-to-end integrity, replay protection, authentication or confidentiality. The RFC lists these threats: message editing, attribute editing, theft of passwords, theft and modification of accounting data, replay attacks, connection hijacking and fraudulent accounting.

Examples: an Access-Accept could be swapped for an Access-Reject and the NAS cannot detect it; EAP or tunnel attributes could be removed so the client uses a weaker method; with PAP, every proxy on the path sees the cleartext password; and a rogue proxy could submit accounting records for sessions that never happened. Reconciling accounting against authentication logs, using the Class attribute, helps detect that. The memo notes that IPSEC ESP can prevent snooping on the wire.
sections.plainLanguage: Every desk on the way can read and change your note, so you have to trust all of them, and that is risky when they belong to different companies.
